newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hoechst settles claims from 1993 accident.
newsitem.headline: Hoechst settles claims from 1993 accident.

text.p: German chemicals and drugs group Hoechst AG has settled all outstanding litigation related to a 1993 industrial accident where toxic substances spewed from a suburban plant, a Frankfurt prosecutor said on Friday.

Relieved the lingering legal battle, which had cost the world's biggest chemicals group over 36 million marks in damages, was finally over, investors sent the group's shares up over two percent in bourse trade.
A Hoechst spokesman said the group was happy the dragged- out process has now been ended.

Prosecutors had charged Hoechst with endangering the environment, causing bodily harm, and failing to inform its workers or the public after toxic chemicals escaped from a plant in the Frankfurt suburb of Griesheim in February 1993.
Ten tonnes of the toxic colour preparation o-Nitroanisol leaked from the plant contaminating nearby streets and sending 30 people to hospital for treatment.

A similar accident occurred at the same plant last January when one tonne of a toxic substance dusted the surrounding neighbourhood after an accident with pressurised equipment tore a hole in the plant's roof.

The prosecutor's office said one employee had been handed a suspended six month jail term for ignoring his shift supervisor's orders by turning on a certain piece of equipment during his overnight shift, helping cause the 1993 accident.
Prosecutors charged that Hoechst had been negligent in its duties to inform the public fully and immediately by announcing it six hours later and downplaying the possible dangers.
Hoechst at the time initially advised people to wear gloves to protect themselves from the slick, yellowish substance and merely to wash their shoes if they came into contact with it.
The group's seemingly cavalier treatment of the accident prompted public outrage and severely strained relations between area residents and one of the region's biggest employers.
Only after relentless public demands did Hoechst cobble together a comprehensive clean-up programme, which included carting off the contaminated earth from local fields and gardens.
After several more smaller incidents, all occurring around the same time, the chemicals giant launched a massive overhaul of its safety procedures, prompting praise from the prosecutor's office.

Last year, still reeling from the negative publicity of three years ago, Hoechst handled the accident aftermath much more aggressively, immediately warning the public, dispatching senior officials to the site and holding detailed briefings.

To settle litigation against the head of the plant and the shift supervisor Hoechst agreed to pay out 500,000 marks after having already paid some 35.75 million marks in compensation in connection with the accident.

The group also pledged to donate another 500,000 marks to the community. "We are relieved and expect that this will be an additional step to improve our relations with the local residents," a Hoechst spokesman said.
Hoechst shares ended bourse trade up 1.40 marks at 65 marks while the broader index closed up nearly one percentage point at 3,244.93.
